title: Proteomics from Triple-Negative Breast Cancer from the MMTV-R26Met Model
projectDescription: We have developed the MMTV-R26Met mouse model, which exclusively generates TNBC and recapitulates key features of the human disease in an immunocompetent setting. In this study, we provide a proteomics characterization of MMTV-R26Met-derived tumors. This integrative approach reveals distinct tumor clusters that reflect patient-like heterogeneity and provides a valuable framework for TNBC stratification and therapeutic development.
sampleProcessingProtocol: For protein extraction, cell pellets were lysed with RIPA buffer, with the buffer volume adjusted to the cell count to achieve a concentration of approximately 1 µg/ul (assuming 1x10^6 cells yield 50ug of protein). A theoretical maximum of 20 µg of protein was used for proteomics experiments. For samples yielding less than 20ug, the entire sample was used after dilution with lithium dodecyl sulfate (LDS) sample buffer to a final volume of 20 µl Samples were stacked on NuPAGE™ gel in a single band, followed by trypsin digestion prior to mass spectrometry analysis using an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid Mass Spectrometer (ThermoFisher Scientific) in data-independent acquisition mode (DIA).
dataProcessingProtocol: Protein identification and quantification were processed using the DIA-NN 1.8.2 beta27 algorithm (Demichev et al. 2020) and DIAgui package (https://github.com/marseille-proteomique/DIAgui,(Gerault, Camoin, et Granjeaud 2024)).  Statistical analyses were carried out using the Perseus software (version 1.6.15.0). Proteins were pre-filtered to exclude contaminants and those with less than 70% valid quantitative values across treatment groups. Missing values were then imputed using Perseus’s normal distribution imputation method (Width: 0.3, Down shift: 1.8). Differential protein expression was assessed using a two-sample t-test, applying a permutation-based false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.05 with 250 iterations, and with a log2 fold change threshold set at <-1.5 or > 1.5 (Tyanova et Cox 2018).
